q: In HCI, what is context also known as, and what does it focus on?
options: Interface; the colors and icons of a system
Paradigm; how the human-computer interaction will be formed
Prototype; the first working model of a system
Framework; the programming language used
explanation: Context is also known as paradigm. It focuses on how the HCI will be formed and investigates strategies for building interactive, usable systems.

q: What does the User Interface (UI) focus on?
options: How easy it is to navigate between pages
Identifying features, constraints, and quality assurance
The rate of communication between user and system
The look, feel, presentation, and interactivity of the system
explanation: UI covers the look, feel, presentation, and interactivity of a system. Navigation ease and quality assurance belong to UX, and the rate of communication is responsiveness.

q: What does User Experience (UX) focus on?
options: How the user interacts with the system
Only the colors and fonts of the system
The hardware the system runs on
The number of icons on a screen
explanation: UX focuses on how the user interacts with the system, such as how easy it is to reach a page and to use the system without help. Colors and fonts are part of UI.

q: What is learnability?
options: The ability of the system to withstand adverse conditions
The ability of the user to customize the interface
The ease with which new users can begin effective interaction and achieve maximal performance
The ability to run more than one task at a time
explanation: Learnability is how easily new users can start using a system well. Withstanding adverse conditions is robustness, customizing is customizability, and many tasks at once is multithreading.

q: What is predictability in interaction design?
options: The user's ability to assess the effect of past operations
The user's ability to foresee the operations that can be performed next
The system's ability to recover from errors
The use of real-world objects as icons
explanation: Predictability is about foreseeing what can be done next and what the outcome will be. Assessing past operations is synthesizability.

q: What is synthesizability?
options: Support for the user to assess the effect of past operations on the current state
The ability to substitute equivalent input and output values
Consistency among different applications
The ability of the user to change themes and colors
explanation: Synthesizability helps the user understand what past actions changed. Substituting input and output is task substitutivity, and consistency across applications is generalizability.

q: What is affordance?
options: Matching user expectations with how real-world objects function
Giving the user another avenue to understand the system
A notification that tells the user what changed
The principle where the appearance of objects suggests how they can be manipulated
explanation: Affordance means an object's appearance shows how to use it. Matching real-world expectations is guessability, and another avenue to understand the system is metaphor.

q: What is generalizability?
options: Likeness in input and output behavior within one system
Passing tasks between user and system
A form of consistency among different applications that lets users of one adapt easily to another similar application
Displaying the current status of a long operation
explanation: Generalizability carries interaction knowledge from one application to similar ones. Likeness within a system is consistency, and passing tasks is task migratability.

q: What is consistency in design principles?
options: Likeness in input and output behavior arising from similar situations or task objectives
The ability to open many windows at once
The system's ability to change itself without the user
The speed at which the system responds
explanation: Consistency is sameness of behavior, terminology, formatting, icons, and labels in similar situations. It supports generalizability.

q: What is multithreading?
options: Passing responsibility for a task between user and system
The ability of a system to support user interaction for more than one task at a time
Modifying the user interface to personal preferences
Recovering from an error by returning to a previous state
explanation: Multithreading supports interaction with more than one task at a time, and can be interleaved or concurrent. The other options describe task migratability, customizability, and backward recovery.

q: What is task migratability?
options: Allowing equivalent input and output values to be swapped
Moving files from one folder to another
Showing loading animations during long tasks
Passing the responsibility of executing tasks between the user and the system
explanation: Task migratability shares task execution between user and system, like a spell checker that suggests but does not force corrections. Swapping input and output is task substitutivity.

q: What is observability?
options: The rate of communication between user and system
The user's ability to reach a goal after an error
The user's ability to evaluate and understand the internal state of the system from its perceivable representation
The use of appearance to make a system familiar
explanation: Observability lets the user understand what the system is doing, for example through a loading bar. The rate of communication is responsiveness, and reaching a goal after an error is recoverability.

q: Which list gives the elements of graphic design?
options: Color and texture; line, shape, and form; space and size; typography
Balance; proximity and alignment; contrast; repetition and movement; white space
Predictability; synthesizability; familiarity; generalizability; consistency
Observability; recoverability; responsiveness
explanation: The elements are the building blocks: color and texture, line, shape, and form, space and size, and typography. The second list is the factors of graphic design, and the others are learnability and robustness factors.

q: Which list gives the factors of graphic design?
options: Color and texture; line and shape; space and size; typography
Balance; proximity and alignment; contrast; repetition and movement; white space
Multithreading; task migratability; task substitutivity; customizability
Guessability; metaphor; affordance
explanation: The factors are balance, proximity and alignment, contrast, repetition and movement, and white space. The first list is the elements, the third is flexibility factors, and the last is familiarity concepts.

q: Predictability is often referred to as what?
options: Immediate honesty
Task conformance
Operation visibility
Recognition over recall
explanation: Predictability is often called operation visibility: if an operation can be performed, there should be a clear indication of it, and user actions should be matched by a response.

q: What is the relationship between UI and UX?
options: UX is a part of UI
They are the same thing
UI and UX are unrelated
UI is a part of UX
explanation: UI is a part of UX. UI is graphic design (presenting information aesthetically), while UX is system analysis (features, constraints, quality assurance).

q: What do 4xx webpage error codes indicate?
options: Client errors
Server errors
The client must take additional action to complete the request
The page loaded successfully
explanation: 4xx codes are client errors, such as 404 page not found. 5xx codes are server errors, and 3xx codes mean the client must take additional action.

q: In customizability, what is the difference between adaptability and adaptivity?
options: Adaptability is done by the system; adaptivity is done by the user
Adaptability is modification by the user; adaptivity is modification by the system
Both mean the system cannot be changed
Adaptability is for mobile; adaptivity is for desktop
explanation: Customizability is modifiability by the user (adaptability) or by the system (adaptivity). Swapping them is a common mistake.

q: What is recoverability?
options: The rate of communication between user and system
Showing the user that an operation is available
Keeping the same icons across applications
The user's ability to reach a desired goal after recognizing errors in a previous interaction
explanation: Recoverability lets the user still reach the goal after an error, through forward (negotiation) or backward (undo) recovery.

q: What is task substitutivity?
options: Passing tasks between user and system
Running tasks one at a time
Allowing equivalent values of input and output to be substituted for each other
Letting the user change the font size
explanation: Task substitutivity lets equivalent input and output values replace each other, blurring the line between input and output, like typing line coordinates or drawing the line and seeing its coordinates.

q: What is responsiveness?
options: A measure of the rate of communication between the user and the system
The ability to undo a mistake
The use of highly recognizable icons
The ability to work on one document at a time
explanation: Responsiveness measures how quickly the user and system communicate; a short, instantaneous response time is more desirable.

q: Which are the three familiarity concepts?
options: Immediate honesty, eventual honesty, observability
Guessability, metaphor, affordance
Interleaved, concurrent, customizable
Forward, backward, responsive
explanation: The familiarity concepts are guessability (matching real-world expectations), metaphor (another avenue to understand the system), and affordance (appearance suggests use).

q: Which pairing of an example and its concept is mismatched?
options: Highlighted pasted files in the new folder: immediate honesty
Undo button in Word: backward recovery
Floppy disk save icon: familiarity
Command Prompt giving no success or failure feedback: immediate honesty
explanation: The Command Prompt is an example of eventual honesty: there is no feedback, so the user must double check the result. The other pairs are correct.

q: Which statement about an interleaved system is NOT true?
options: It permits work on a single task at a given time
Multiple windows can be open at the same time
It allows multiple tasks to be actioned at the same time
A word processor with many open documents but one active is an example
explanation: Actioning many tasks at the same time describes a concurrent system. An interleaved system has many tasks open but only one being worked on at any instant.

q: Which pairing of an example and its recovery type is mismatched?
options: Undo button: forward recovery
Username kept after a rejected password: forward recovery
Word document recovery of autosaved files: backward recovery
Returning to a previous state to remove an undesired outcome: backward recovery
explanation: Undo returns to a previous state, so it is backward recovery. Forward recovery works from the current state toward the goal, like keeping the username after a wrong password.

q: Which is NOT one of the factors that affect learnability?
options: Predictability
Observability
Familiarity
Generalizability
explanation: Observability is a factor of robustness. The learnability factors are predictability, synthesizability, familiarity, generalizability, and consistency.

q: Which statement about robustness and observability is NOT true?
options: Robustness is the ability to withstand or overcome adverse conditions
Loading elements reassure the user that a process has not crashed
If users cannot understand a product's state, their opinion of it will be negative
5xx error codes indicate client errors
explanation: 5xx codes indicate server errors; 4xx codes are client errors. The other statements are correct.

q: A user types the wrong password on a login page. The page shows an error but keeps the username filled in, so the user only re-enters the password. Which concept does this show?
options: Forward (negotiation) recovery
Backward (undo) recovery
Eventual honesty
Task substitutivity
explanation: The user works from the current state toward the goal instead of starting over, which is forward recovery. Backward recovery would return to an earlier state.

q: A gamer talks to friends on Discord while playing a game, and both keep running at the same time. Which type of multithreading is this?
options: Interleaved system
Concurrent system
Task migratability
Customizability
explanation: Several tasks are actioned at the same time, which is a concurrent system. In an interleaved system only one task is active at a time.

q: Most save icons look like a floppy disk, which users recognize from old storage media. Which learnability factor does this show?
options: Predictability
Synthesizability
Familiarity
Consistency
explanation: Familiarity applies the user's prior knowledge to a new system; the appearance of the floppy disk tells users what the icon does.
